findings.title: `unset` routing contradicts the collision remediation and walkthrough step 9
findings.description:
Line 89 says delete "mirrors write" and that `migrate-personal` is "the one exception that touches the *other* project file". For a personal key, `cf config unset git.integration_branch --project` therefore deletes from `.context-forge.local.toml`.

Lines 146 and 259 rely on that same command to clear the stale copy in the shared file. Under the design's own routing, step 9 does the opposite:

- It removes the personal value (`legacy/value`), which the collision rule exists to protect.
- The read then falls through to the stale shared value (`another-legacy-value`).
- The `cf check` warning stays, so "confirm `cf check` is clean again" cannot pass.

The CLI surface is frozen (line 37), so no command can remove a personal key from the shared file after a collision skip. The finding becomes permanent short of hand-editing.

The same root cause produces a silent no-op before migration. With the value only in the shared file, `unset --project` reports success and the value still resolves.

Lightest fix: on collision, have `migrate-personal` keep the personal value, delete the shared copy and report both values. The personal value already wins at read time, and the discarded one stays in git history. This drops the "skipped" state and the follow-up `unset` step. Separately, state what `delete` does for a personal key that exists only in the shared file: either remove it from both files or fail explicitly.

findings.title: Migration silently drops the value for every other checkout once committed
findings.description:
`migrate-personal` moves the key into a gitignored file and deletes it from a committed one. When that developer commits the shared-file change, each teammate who pulls has no personal file and no shared value. `git.integration_branch` resolves to the empty default, and their work branches fork from and merge into `main`.

Nothing surfaces this. The new checker rule only looks for personal keys in the shared file, and there are none left. That breaks the design's own requirement at line 138 ("Reads must not silently drop that value out from under the user") and the claim at line 264 that "nothing breaks silently". The slice plan's "defined migration/compat story" is unmet for the multi-developer case.

The effect is inherent to the move, so the design need not prevent it, but it must make it visible. At minimum the `migrate-personal` report should state that committing the shared-file change removes the value for all other checkouts and that each developer must set their own. Add the effect to Risk Assessment.

findings.title: Gitignore coverage only reaches freshly initialized projects
findings.description:
The only mechanism that ignores `.context-forge.local.toml` is `cf init`. Projects that already exist are the same population the Migration Plan targets, and they get the file created by `cf config set ... --project` or `migrate-personal` with no ignore entry. A routine `git add -A` then commits it, which is the leak this slice exists to close.

The Overview (line 19) promises `cf check` "enough awareness to keep personal settings out of git", but the one new rule does not look at whether the personal file is ignored.

Lightest fix: reuse the same ensure-ignored helper whenever `ConfigManager` or the CLI first creates the personal file, including in `migrate-personal`. Alternatively, add a `cf check` warning when the personal file exists and is not ignored.

findings.title: Listed tests omit the behaviours the design spends most words defining
Read path is classification-gated where a uniform chain would do
findings.description:
The condition in step 2 is true in every case (a shared key, or a personal key not found in step 1), so it adds wording without behaviour. The slice plan asks to reuse "the existing user-vs-project two-file-precedence merge pattern". A uniform personal → shared → user → default lookup for every key does that, and the migration fallback follows from it with no special case.

As written, a shared key hand-placed in the local file is silently ignored. That is surprising given the design invokes the `.env.local` convention at line 113. Pick one behaviour and state it; if such keys are ignored, a symmetric checker finding would make it visible.

findings.title: Small under-specified details
findings.description:
- **Exit status:** the design does not say whether `migrate-personal` exits non-zero when any key reports `failed:`. Exiting zero on partial failure hides it from scripts.
- **Gitignore match:** line 159 allows a "substring" check, which would match a comment or a negation line (`!.context-forge.local.toml`). Use trimmed whole-line equality.
- **MCP field name:** the API Contracts section does not name the new `config_get` `configPaths` field for the personal path, although it specifies every other contract.
- **Per-key failure handling:** continue-past-failure across keys (line 149) is machinery for a registry with one personal key. Reading both files once and writing personal then shared gives the same safe ordering with less code.

findings.title: Scope matches the slice plan entry
findings.description: Every element of the 915 entry is present: `scope` on `CONFIG_KEYS`, per-key file routing through `ConfigManager` and `configPaths`, the one-line `cf init` gitignore addition, a migration story, and the MCP config tools. The broader gitignore scaffolding is correctly left to Future Work. Nothing assigned to the slice is dropped, and the effort matches the plan's 3/5.

findings.title: Layering and dependency direction
findings.description: Routing lives in core `ConfigManager`, keyed off the registry, with unchanged public signatures. CLI and MCP stay thin consumers and dependencies still point toward core. A required `scope` field with no default forces an explicit classification for every future key and avoids a silent fallback. Keeping the migration out of the closed `fixAction` union is the lighter and correct choice.

findings.title: Failure modes enumerated for the new write paths
findings.description: The `migrate-personal` write-then-delete ordering, the personal-file write and the `.gitignore` read-modify-write each have an explicit strategy that fails loudly. The parent architecture states no NFRs for this path, so none need restating.
